overview: Afghanistan’s modern history grew out of the Durrani realm founded in 1747 and its gradual contraction into a territorial state. This card follows a country through changing monarchies, republics and Taliban governments. It also follows the people who baked bread, taught children, cared for patients and protected collections through those changes. The map’s 1783 start is a coverage date, not the country’s founding.

periods.title: Durrani inheritance and fragmentation
periods.summary: Ahmad Shah’s successors inherited a large, increasingly divided realm.

periods.summary: Dost Mohammad’s rise and two British invasions reshaped the state.

periods.title: Centralization and external constraints
periods.summary: Abdur Rahman and Habibullah strengthened government; foreign relations remained constrained.

periods.title: Independent monarchy and reform
periods.summary: Amanullah’s reforms preceded later kings, including Zahir Shah and the 1964 constitution.

periods.title: Daoud’s republic
periods.summary: The overthrow of the monarchy established a republic.

periods.title: Communist governments and war
periods.summary: The 1978 coup preceded Soviet intervention in 1979 and withdrawal in 1989.

periods.title: Islamic State and factional war
periods.summary: Rival armed groups fought after the communist government’s collapse.

periods.title: First Taliban government
periods.summary: The Taliban controlled most of Afghanistan before the 2001 intervention.

periods.summary: An elected government developed with international support amid continuing war.

periods.summary: Taliban rule returned in 2021; dated examples here extend through 2026.

sections.title: A changing country on a coarse map

items.text: The map’s Afghanistan outline changes sharply: its 1783 and 1800 snapshots extend much farther west or east than its later outline. One later snapshot covers 1960 to 1994, crossing several governments. These shapes cannot show every change of control, and the imported name “Islamic State of Afghanistan” fits only part of this long history.

Ahmad Shah Durrani established his realm in 1747. At its height it reached from Central Asia toward the Indian Ocean and northern India, but tribute and allegiance did not make every district equally obedient. Sikh expansion, local resistance and succession struggles weakened this enormous inheritance.

Abdur Rahman’s reign, from 1880 to 1901, strengthened central power through troops, taxation and controls on local leaders. This came at a severe human cost: campaigns in Hazarajat caused repression and exile, while the conquest of Kafiristan imposed conversion to Islam and the new name Nuristan.

State-building also brought roads, bridges, caravanserais and small industries employing foreign technical specialists. A public clinic opened in 1895. These changes were concentrated in Kabul, so a new machine or clinic in the capital did not mean every village suddenly had one.

After the Third Anglo-Afghan War, the 1919 settlement secured independence in foreign affairs. Amanullah introduced a constitution in 1923, but resistance to his reforms helped force his abdication in 1929. Independence and domestic agreement were very different achievements.

In 2001 a United States-led campaign against al-Qaeda and the Taliban removed the first Taliban government. The internationally supported government that followed made uneven gains while a Taliban insurgency continued. In August 2021, as foreign forces withdrew and government forces collapsed, the Taliban entered Kabul and President Ashraf Ghani fled.

sections.title: Books, classrooms and a Persian writing sample

items.text: Writing history was itself political work. Fayz Muhammad compiled Siraj al-Tawarikh in Kabul under Emir Habibullah’s supervision. Its early volumes covered earlier rulers; the third drew closely on government orders, letters and documents. Such books preserve valuable evidence while also showing what a ruler allowed an author to say.

A short Persian writing sample is the title سراج التواریخ, transliterated Sirāj al-tawārīkh, meaning “Lamp of history.” This is modern typesetting of the title in Fayz Muhammad’s early-1910s history, also visible in the Library of Congress text. It is a dated example of written Persian used for Afghan history, among Afghanistan’s many languages.

One small schoolbook makes education tangible: the Library of Congress holds a 28-page Persian Islamic-education textbook prepared for Afghan elementary pupils. Its catalog tentatively dates the Lahore printing to about 1913 and records approval by Afghan religious and education authorities. School knowledge could travel across a border in a very thin book.

The Islamic Republic’s 2004 constitution recognized gender equality and reserved parliamentary seats for women. UN Women reports that women held 69 of 249 parliamentary seats by 2021. These were institutions of that former republic; the change of government later that year profoundly altered women’s public lives.

UNESCO reported in August 2026 that about 2.4 million girls were excluded from secondary education under Taliban restrictions, while women were barred from university. Nearly one million girls had been enrolled in secondary education in 2021. This reversal concerns real classrooms, friendships and ambitions, not just a number on a chart.

Learning efforts continued under these restrictions. UNESCO’s August 2026 account describes community literacy, skills classes and psychosocial support, while emphasizing that these alternatives cannot replace normal access to school. The primary-school examples below therefore should not be mistaken for evidence that older girls could freely continue their education.

Nancy Hatch Dupree’s 1993 account links hospitality and family celebrations with cooking, while stressing regional diversity and the simplicity of many everyday meals. A feast for guests could be much more elaborate than supper on an ordinary evening. Bread and sweetened black or green tea were central staples in her account.

Bread did not always need a kitchen oven. Dupree describes dough baked against a clay oven’s walls, nomadic groups using a curved iron griddle, and shepherds wrapping dough around heated stones beside a fire. A hot rock could be useful cooking equipment, though rather awkward to put in a kitchen drawer.

Food could also express thanks. Dupree describes sweets distributed after prayers were answered and rice dishes given to people visiting religious shrines. Some shrines kept enormous cooking vessels and employed cooks for these gatherings. These are documented late-twentieth-century practices, not a claim that every Afghan household observed the same customs.

Restorers in Kabul’s Murad Khani district had to remove so much accumulated garbage that street levels fell by as much as two metres. Some families had been confined to upper floors. As the debris came out, old houses reappeared: restoring a neighborhood began with the decidedly unglamorous work of hauling rubbish.

Murad Khani’s nineteenth-century courtyards also became classrooms for craft. Turquoise Mountain reports training builders in woodwork and mud plaster, restoring carved cedar panels, and converting buildings into a library and spaces for ceramics, calligraphy and miniature painting. One restored serai received a UNESCO conservation award in 2013.

sections.title: Care, water and the everyday work of staying well

items.text: In a 2015 WHO report, Dr Aziza worked as a midwife in a mobile clinic serving 450 displaced families in Kabul’s Nasaji-Bagrami camp. The clinic was operated by an Afghan organization, SHRDO. Her account describes more women seeking family-planning and hygiene advice: medical care included conversation and trust as well as treatment.

At Malik Sheer Ahmed school in Logar, a teacher recalled children leaving to relieve themselves in fields or missing lessons to fetch water. UNICEF’s July 2025 report describes new toilets and handwashing facilities. Six-year-old Malika especially liked having soap and a place to wash indoors. A usable school toilet can be an educational improvement.

In Bamyan’s Qafila Bashi village, a 2025 water project supplied a reservoir for 130 households, with taps shared by four or five families. Safoora’s children, Zahra and Abdul Ahad, could attend primary school without the old task of fetching water from a stream four kilometres away. Household chores and classroom time were closely connected.

sections.title: Discovering and protecting a deeper past

items.text: In 1978, excavators at Tillya Tepe uncovered six richly furnished ancient graves. Among the finds was a first-century CE gold crown that could be folded for transport. The discovery belongs to modern archaeological history; the crown belongs to people who lived long before the modern Afghan state. Royal luggage apparently needed practical solutions too.

Museum workers later protected important collections by moving objects into safer storage and keeping valuable pieces hidden. Their survival was publicly announced in 2003; authentication and inventory followed in 2004. The Art Gallery of New South Wales records the work of Afghan curators and archaeologists alongside foreign specialists. Preservation was an achievement of people, not only institutions.

That survival was incomplete. A rocket attack badly damaged the National Museum in 1993, and looting removed many objects and records. In 2001 the Taliban destroyed museum sculptures and the great Bamiyan Buddhas. Conservators later helped reassemble damaged pieces; an old fragment could become evidence again instead of remaining rubble.

ending.text: Afghanistan continues through changes of government. The Islamic Republic collapsed in August 2021 and the Taliban returned to power; that political ending did not mean the disappearance of Afghanistan’s people.
